prompt: A woman you casually know spots you as you walk through a store , approaches you , smiles and says , `` I saw your gravestone today , just lovely ! '' and nonchalantly strolls away .
content:
### Just Lovely

I was choosing between two jars of mustard when Marlene Pike found me.

We knew each other in the way people know each other in small towns: by name, by face, and by the vague impression that we’d once stood near each other at a school fundraiser. She came up the aisle with a basket hooked over one arm, smiling as if we’d arranged to meet.

“I saw your gravestone today,” she said. “Just lovely!”

Then she strolled away.

I stood holding the mustard.

I couldn’t decide whether she’d made a joke, confused me with someone else, or finally lost whatever sense of tact she’d had. Marlene had always been a little odd—she wore gardening gloves to the bakery in spring, and once told me my daughter had “a face that belonged in an old photograph.” But this was a new level.

I set down the mustard and went after her.

She’d turned into the next aisle. By the time I reached it, she was gone.

At the checkout, I asked the cashier if she’d seen Marlene leave.

“Who?” he said, still scanning my groceries.

I decided not to answer.

The cemetery was on my way home, though I hadn’t meant to stop. I told myself I wanted to see if Marlene had mistaken me for someone else. Plenty of people shared my name. There might be a Mrs. Eleanor Voss buried there, and Marlene, being Marlene, had found the stone lovely and thought I’d appreciate the news.

The cemetery gates were open. I followed the gravel path past the old maples, reading names without meaning to. At the far end, where the ground rose gently toward the church, I saw the fresh flowers first.

White lilies. My daughter’s choice.

Then I saw the stone.

ELEANOR VOSS  
1958–2024

The letters were cut deep and clean into pale granite. A small carved wren perched above my name. I liked wrens. I’d once told my daughter that they looked as if they were always in a hurry to get somewhere important.

Below the dates, someone had added:

SHE MADE A HOME WHEREVER SHE WAS.

I read it twice.

My hands went cold. I looked down at my own hands, expecting them to be trembling. They weren’t. They looked exactly as they always had—freckles, wedding ring, a small burn mark near my thumb from the year I’d tried to make caramel.

I touched the stone.

It was warm from the sun.

Behind me, a car crunched over the gravel. I turned. My daughter, Lucy, got out and shut the door. She carried a paper cup of coffee and wore the blue coat I’d given her for Christmas.

She came to the grave and stood very still.

“I got the one you would’ve liked,” she said.

I wanted to tell her the wren was perfect. I wanted to ask who had written the words. I wanted to tell her that I was right there, right beside her, and that she didn’t have to come every week.

Lucy set the coffee down among the lilies.

Then she took a little brass key from her pocket and laid it on the stone.

My key. The one to the house I’d left her.

“I can’t keep going in there yet,” she whispered. “Not without you.”

And then I remembered.

The rain. The red light. The truck that slid through the intersection as if the road belonged to it.

Lucy put her palm against the stone. I put mine over hers, though I could feel nothing but the sun.

For a moment, she bowed her head. Then she picked up the coffee and walked back to her car.

At the gate, Marlene Pike stood waiting. She watched Lucy go, then glanced toward me. This time she didn’t smile.

I understood, finally, what she had seen in the store.

I looked once more at the stone, at the careful letters and the wren in flight.

It was lovely.

### The Last Lottery

I had narrowed the successor list to three hundred and twelve names when the letter arrived.

It slid beneath the door of my rooms in the old observatory, leaving a dark, sticky streak across the floor. The handwriting was unmistakable, though the letters wavered as if written in a moving carriage.

**We are the only ones left.**

It was written in blood.

I knew the hand. I knew the blood, too.

For a long while, I sat at my desk with the letter open before me and the brass bowl full of names beside it. Three hundred and twelve slips. One draw. One stranger chosen to inherit the Harbor’s strength, its endless years, its obligation to stand between the world and whatever came to break it.

I had planned to let chance decide.

Now I folded the letter and went to find Mara.

I found her in the ruined railway station where we had once stopped an army by holding up a bridge. She sat beneath the clock, one hand wrapped in a blood-soaked bandage. The wound was deep, but she looked annoyed rather than afraid.

“You always were dramatic,” I said.

“You always were slow.” She nodded at the letter in my hand. “You got it.”

“I did. What happened?”

“A roof came down. I held it up long enough for the children to get out.” She glanced at her bandage. “Turns out even heroes can still bleed.”

“But not die.”

“Not unless we choose someone to take our place.”

The rule was older than any of us. Older than the names people had given us, older than the songs. A hero could be crushed, burned, pierced through the heart. The world might break them in every way but one. We died only when we chose someone else to carry the work.

And, sometimes, the chosen refused.

That was how we had become so few. Our friends had passed their mantles to people who wanted nothing to do with them. The old heroes died. The line ended. One by one, the names disappeared from the sky.

Mara and I had never chosen.

“We’re the only ones left,” she said.

“I know.”

“No,” she said. “You know there are two names on the list. You don’t know what that means.”

She looked at the bandage on her hand. The blood had seeped through again.

“It means the world is running out of people who remember what this costs.”

I thought of the bowl in my study. “I thought choosing at random might be fair.”

“Fair to whom?”

“To everyone whose name I don’t know.”

“And to the person whose name you draw?”

I had no answer.

Mara stood, wincing. “Come with me.”

She took me to a shelter set up in the basement of a school. The roof had collapsed in the storm, and the town’s people were still bringing blankets, water, and food. In the middle of it all, a young woman moved from cot to cot, checking pulses and tying splints. She had a bruise darkening one cheek. Her hands were steady.

“Who is she?” I asked.

“Lena Vale. She was in the station when the roof fell. She got the children out.”

“Is she on my list?”

“Probably.”

“That isn’t the same as knowing her.”

“No,” Mara said. “It isn’t.”

We waited until the last child had stopped crying. Then I asked Lena to speak with us outside.

I told her what I was. I told her what the Harbor could do, and what it could not. I told her she would not grow old while she held the mantle. I told her that if she ever chose a successor, she would die.

She listened without interrupting.

When I finished, she looked through the doorway at the crowded basement.

“Would I have to leave?” she asked.

“No,” I said. “You could stay.”

“Would I have to save everyone?”

“No one can.”

“Would I have to try?”

“Yes.”

She gave a small, tired smile. “Then I don’t need forever. I need to get through tonight.”

“That isn’t an answer,” Mara said.

“It’s the only one I have.”

It was more than I had expected.

prompt: Reddit , as a collective entity , runs for president .
content:
At 2:13 a.m. on a Tuesday, Reddit announced it was running for president.

The announcement appeared in a red banner at the top of every page:

**WE ARE PLEASED TO ANNOUNCE OUR CANDIDACY.**

Within minutes, someone had made a subreddit to discuss it. Within an hour, there were six competing subreddits, three conspiracy theories, and a petition demanding that the announcement be taken down for being “low effort.”

By morning, Reddit had a campaign logo: a white Snoo wearing a tiny flag as a cape. Its slogan was **A BETTER WORLD IS POSSIBLE, PROBABLY**.

At the first debate, the moderator asked what Reddit would do about housing.

“We believe housing is a human right,” said Reddit.

A second voice cut in: “Not if people keep moving to my city.”

A third voice said, “This is a landlord question.”

A fourth demanded proof that houses were real.

The moderator blinked. “So what is your policy?”

Reddit paused for eleven seconds.

“Depends what you mean by ‘policy,’” it answered.

The clip went viral. The campaign called it a victory for transparency.

Reddit’s rallies were enormous. People gathered in parks, town squares, and the parking lots of closed shopping centers, all holding phones aloft. The candidate addressed them through a wall of screens. Sometimes the speech was stirring.

“We can do better than this,” Reddit said.

Sometimes it was not.

“Your mother was a hamster,” Reddit said once, before a moderator found the source of the audio and removed it.

The other candidates mocked the campaign’s lack of a body, a history, or even a consistent opinion. Reddit replied that these were precisely the features voters wanted in a president.

It promised to listen to everyone. Then it introduced a system in which the loudest voices rose to the top.

It promised to protect free speech. Then it banned the word “ban” for being divisive.

It promised to bring people together. Then it discovered that people preferred arguing in separate rooms.

On election night, Reddit’s campaign headquarters was a server farm in Virginia. Volunteers watched the returns scroll across a wall of monitors. The numbers moved slowly, then all at once.

Reddit won.

The country celebrated, panicked, or posted a meme about it, depending on the subreddit.

On inauguration day, the new president arrived at the Capitol as a live stream. The oath was read aloud. Reddit repeated it in thousands of voices, some solemn, some sarcastic, one apparently playing a harmonica.

Then came the first signature.

The Constitution required the president’s name.

The clerk held out a pen toward the nearest screen.

Reddit went quiet.

For the first time since announcing its candidacy, it had no immediate reply. Somewhere, across millions of open tabs, people waited.

At last, one user typed: “We should each sign.”

The suggestion rose to the top.

Then someone objected that not everyone had voted for Reddit. Someone else pointed out that plenty of voters had been bots. A moderator locked the thread. Another moderator unlocked it. The page refreshed.

The clerk asked, “Who speaks for you?”

Reddit’s Snoo stared from the screen, smiling its simple, unhelpful smile.

“We do,” it said.

“But who is ‘we’?”

A new comment appeared beneath the livestream.

**good question**

It received one upvote. Then two. Then a thousand.

The inauguration crowd began to laugh—not because the answer was funny, but because it was the first honest thing the new president had said.

Reddit signed the document with a single red dot.

It looked, to the clerk, very much like a period.

prompt: A group of fantasy creatures are playing a table top game together where they pretend to be modern-day humans
content:
The game began at sunset, when the last strip of light slipped beneath the mountains and the tavern’s windows turned black as mirrors.

“Everyone ready?” asked Mira.

She sat at the head of the table with a stack of papers, three pencils, and the solemn expression of a queen about to declare war. Which was fitting, since Mira was a queen—of the goblins, though she had left her crown at home.

Around the table sat her friends: Brindle the dragon, folded carefully into a chair built for someone much smaller; Tallow the ghost, hovering just above his seat; Soot the troll, who had brought a bowl of rocks to snack on; and Pip, a fox-folk bard wearing round spectacles he didn’t need.

“Tonight,” Mira announced, “you are all ordinary humans living in a modern city.”

Brindle raised a claw. “How ordinary?”

“You work in an office.”

The dragon’s eyes gleamed. “Is this the adventure where I burn the office down?”

“No,” said Mira.

“Then how do we win?”

“You don’t win. You try to keep your jobs.”

Brindle slumped. “Cruel magic.”

Mira handed out character sheets. Brindle’s human was named Greg and worked in accounting. Soot was Dennis, a building manager. Tallow played a person named Emily, who had recently discovered she was technically alive again and was trying not to make it weird. Pip was Kevin, a freelance graphic designer.

Pip adjusted his unnecessary glasses. “I can do Kevin. I have known several Kevins.”

The adventure began in a gray office building on a rainy Monday morning. Their characters were all late to work because the subway had stopped between stations.

“What do we do?” asked Soot.

“You’re in the office lobby,” said Mira. “Your boss is waiting by the elevator. He looks angry.”

“I walk up to him,” said Soot.

“Dennis walks up,” Mira corrected.

“Right. Dennis walks up. I do not stomp.”

He tried a careful little step. The table shook anyway.

“What’s your excuse for being late?” Mira asked.

Soot considered. “The elevator was full.”

“You arrived by subway.”

“I was going to say the elevator in the subway.”

“That’s not a thing.”

“It is in Dennis’s building.”

Mira scribbled something on her notes. “Fine. Your boss says, ‘You’re forty minutes late, Dennis.’”

“I tell him the truth. The subway stopped.”

“Roll to see whether he believes you.”

Soot rolled a die. It came up a two.

“He says, ‘That’s the third time this month.’”

“It’s been a bad month,” Soot said.

Brindle leaned forward. “Greg enters dramatically.”

“Greg is already there,” Mira said.

“Then he enters more dramatically.”

The dragon rolled his die and got a natural twenty.

Mira blinked. “Greg walks into the lobby carrying four coffees. He has bought the exact drink each person likes, including the boss. Somehow, this makes him seem responsible.”

Brindle looked pleased. “I am good at being human.”

“You’re good at carrying coffee,” said Pip.

They made it upstairs. They answered emails. They sat through a meeting about improving workplace efficiency, during which Brindle’s Greg suggested replacing the office chairs with treasure chests.

“People would sit straighter,” he argued.

“They would also have to sit on treasure,” said Pip.

“Exactly.”

The biggest challenge came at lunchtime. Kevin had forgotten his lunch. Emily had brought a bag of apples but couldn’t remember how eating worked. Dennis opened the refrigerator and found a note taped to the door:

PLEASE STOP PUTTING ROCKS IN HERE.

Soot looked wounded. “Dennis’s rocks were keeping the lettuce cool.”

“They were not,” said Mira.

“They were cool rocks.”

Meanwhile, Greg had discovered the office microwave. He peered inside as it hummed.

“It’s a tiny furnace,” he whispered.

“Do not breathe fire into it,” Mira warned.

“I wasn’t going to.”

Brindle rolled.

The die landed on a three.

Mira sighed. “Greg puts a metal spoon in the microwave.”

Everyone shouted at once.

“Why did I do that?” Brindle demanded.

“Because you’re playing a human,” said Pip. “You’re supposed to make choices you don’t understand.”

The microwave sparked. The lights flickered. Somewhere in the building, an alarm began to chirp.

Mira looked around the table. “What do you do?”

“I unplug it,” said Tallow.

“You float through the wall and fetch the fire extinguisher,” said Pip.

“I tell everyone to remain calm,” said Soot.

“And I eat the lunch before it catches fire,” said Brindle.

Mira placed a hand over her notes. “All right. The four of you rush to save the break room.”

They rolled dice. Soot’s Dennis heroically pulled the plug. Pip’s Kevin found the extinguisher. Tallow’s Emily guided everyone through the smoke by remembering how lungs worked. Brindle’s Greg rescued the lunches.

When the alarm stopped, their boss appeared in the doorway.

The table fell quiet.

“What does he say?” asked Pip.

Mira checked her notes. Then she smiled.

“He says, ‘Good teamwork. I’m putting you all in charge of the office safety committee.’”

Everyone groaned.

Brindle pushed back from the table. “Can Greg burn the office down now?”

“No,” said Mira. “Now Greg has a committee meeting.”

The dragon covered his face with both wings.

Outside, the real moon rose over the mountains. Inside, the creatures bent over their character sheets, arguing about fire regulations, public transit, and whether a person could legally keep rocks in a refrigerator.

For one evening, none of them were dragons or ghosts or goblins.

They were just coworkers.

And, somehow, that was the strangest adventure of all.

prompt: Hawksbill Mountain
content:
## Hawksbill Mountain

When Mara was nine, her father told her the mountain had a face.

“Look,” he said, pointing across the gorge. “A hawk’s beak.”

She squinted at the long ridge. It looked like a sleeping dog to her, but she nodded. Her father was good at seeing things before they were there: deer in shadows, rain in clear skies, the beginning of a trail where the forest seemed unbroken.

Years later, after he was gone, Mara drove to Hawksbill Mountain with his ashes on the passenger seat.

The urn was smaller than she expected. It wore a screw-top lid and a blue paper label from the funeral home. Her father had always been broad—broad hands, broad laugh, broad opinions about the proper way to sharpen a knife. It seemed wrong that all of him could fit in something she could hold in one hand.

At the trailhead she tucked the urn into her pack. The climb began steeply, between roots and stones. She stopped often, partly to catch her breath and partly because she didn’t know what she was supposed to be thinking. Her father had never asked to be brought here. He had only brought her, once, when she was small.

At the top, she remembered, he had stood with his hands on his hips and made her look back at the mountain from a distant overlook. That was where the face appeared: the blunt crown, the long slope, the rocky point of its beak.

But from the summit there was no face. There was only wind, and the gorge dropping away beneath her in layers of blue-green forest.

Mara set the urn on a flat rock.

She had imagined saying something. Thank you, perhaps. Or I’m sorry. She had practiced both in the car, then disliked the sound of each. Now her mouth was dry and her thoughts had gone quiet.

A hawk rose from the trees below. It climbed without flapping, turning once in the light.

Mara took the lid off the urn.

The wind tugged at her hair. She pictured the ashes scattering over the rocks, over the trees, into the vastness below. She pictured her father becoming part of a place he had loved, and felt, unexpectedly, that he would have objected.

Not to the place. To the ceremony.

He had disliked grand gestures. Once, after she’d made him a birthday card covered in glitter, he’d admired it and then spent twenty minutes trying to get the glitter off his sleeve.

“You don’t have to make a thing into a monument,” he’d told her, though she could no longer remember what they had been talking about.

Mara screwed the lid back on.

Instead, she took his old brass compass from her pocket. The glass was scratched, and the needle wandered before settling. He had carried it on hikes even after phones could do a better job. She turned it over. On the back, in his careful block letters, were the words: **LOOK UP.**

She laughed once, surprised by the sound.

Then she put the compass away and shouldered her pack. The urn went with her.

On the descent, the mountain kept changing shape. From one bend it was a great shoulder of stone. From another, a long dark back under the sky. Only from far away, Mara remembered, did the beak appear.

At the trailhead she took out her phone and called her brother.

“I went up,” she said.

“And?”

“I didn’t leave him there.”

Her brother was quiet for a moment. “Good.”

They agreed to meet the following Sunday at their father’s house. There were boxes to sort, tools to divide, a drawer full of maps neither of them knew how to fold properly.

Before hanging up, Mara looked back through the trees. She couldn’t see Hawksbill Mountain, only the bright spaces between branches.

For the first time that day, she knew exactly what she wanted to say.

“I’ll see you soon,” she said.

And this time, she meant her brother.

prompt: [ NSFW ] The number of times someone has had sex is listed above their heads at all times for everyone to see . Describe a day in the life of a 50 year old virgin .
content:
### The Zero

At fifty, Martin knew that the zero above his head was the first thing most people noticed.

Not always first in the order of their eyes. They might look at his face, his coat, the cup in his hand. But then their gaze would flick up, and there it was: **0**, neat and white as a price tag.

He saw everyone else’s numbers too. His neighbor had **12**. The woman on the bus had **3**. A boy in a school uniform had **0**, and his father walked beside him with **1**, looking as if he expected somebody to make a joke.

Nobody did. Not out loud.

Martin worked in the city library, repairing books that had been loved too hard. He liked the quiet concentration of it: glue, linen tape, a bone folder. The numbers above his coworkers bobbed as they moved between shelves. **6. 24. 1. 0.** They had stopped feeling like revelations years ago. A person’s number told you one fact about them. The trouble was how easily people mistook it for the whole story.

At lunch, his friend Claire sat across from him in the staff room. Her number was **19**. She had once told Martin about each of them, but only because she wanted to. She never asked about his zero.

“Dinner tonight?” she asked.

“With someone from the app.”

Claire raised her eyebrows. “That’s promising.”

“It’s noodles,” Martin said. “Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.”

He had met Ana online three weeks ago. Her profile said she was a landscape architect, liked bad detective shows, and was tired of people treating numbers like horoscopes. Above her head was **8**. Martin had stared at it when they first met for coffee, then apologized for staring. She’d laughed.

“I can’t blame you,” she’d said. “It’s right there.”

Now, before dinner, he stood in his bedroom and considered three shirts. The zero hovered above him in the mirror, as unhelpful as ever.

At the restaurant, Ana arrived in a green jacket and kissed his cheek. Her number was still **8**.

“You look nice,” she said.

“I’m glad. I changed shirts four times.”

“Only four? You’re holding back.”

They talked about work, then about their parents, then about the strange things people said when they saw the numbers. Ana told him a man once congratulated her on **8**, as if she’d won a raffle.

“Did he get a ninth?” Martin asked.

“No. He got a lecture.”

Martin laughed. He liked her laugh: low and surprised, as if it had caught her on its way somewhere else.

After dinner they walked to the river. The city lights trembled in the water. For a while they talked about nothing important. Martin told her how he’d once repaired a book whose owner had pressed a dried flower between its pages. Ana told him about a client who wanted a garden with no plants that attracted bees.

At the footbridge, she stopped.

“Can I ask you something?” she said.

“Of course.”

“Do you want to be a virgin?”

Martin considered the question. He appreciated that she’d asked it plainly.

“I don’t think I ever decided to be one,” he said. “It just kept being true. At some point, I started acting like that meant I’d failed some test. Then I got older, and it seemed harder to explain. Easier not to try.”

Ana nodded. There was no pity in her face, which made it easier to keep looking at her.

“Do you want to have sex?” she asked.

“Yes,” he said, and felt his ears warm. “With you, I mean. If you want to.”

“I do,” she said. “But we can go slowly. And you can change your mind at any point. So can I.”

“Okay.”

They walked to her apartment. On the stairs, Martin’s hands were damp. He thought of all the possible ways to be awkward, and then of the fact that he had already survived the first fifty years of his life.

At her door, Ana turned toward him.

“Still okay?”

“Yes.”

She kissed him. Martin closed his eyes. The numbers disappeared—not because they were gone, but because for once he wasn’t looking up.

Later, in the dimness of her bedroom, they undressed carefully, with pauses and quiet questions. Ana’s hand rested against his chest. His rested at her waist. When they made love, it was not graceful in the way films promised. They bumped knees. Martin laughed once, nervously, and Ana kissed the laugh out of him. They took their time. She asked if he was all right; he said yes, and meant it.

Afterward, lying beside her, he looked up.

The number above his head had changed.

**1.**

Ana’s was still **8**. The digits hovered in the dark like little illuminated signs.

Martin waited for a feeling to arrive: triumph, perhaps, or relief. Something large enough to match the importance he’d given the zero for so long.

Instead, he felt warm. A little dazed. Tired in a pleasant way.

“Are you okay?” Ana asked.

“Yes,” he said. “I am.”

She took his hand.

On the walk home, the night bus was nearly empty. Across the aisle, a woman glanced at Martin’s new **1**, then looked away. He watched the number reflected in the window, hovering over his own faint reflection.

It was still just one fact.

At home, he brushed his teeth, set his alarm, and climbed into bed. The **1** floated above him, visible to anyone who might have cared to look.

For once, Martin didn’t check whether it was still there.

prompt: A person 's final thoughts .
content:
**The Last Light**

The room had gone quiet except for the rain ticking against the window.

Mara had always imagined that dying would feel dramatic—some great door swinging open, perhaps, or a voice calling her name from the other side. Instead, it felt like being very tired after a long day. The blanket was warm. Her hands were cool. Someone had left the bedside lamp on.

Her son sat beside her, asleep in the chair, his chin resting on his chest. He had the same stubborn cowlick he’d had at six, when he insisted he could cut his own hair. Mara smiled at the memory. The uneven fringe. His outrage when she laughed. The way he’d forgiven her by morning.

There were so many things she might have said to him. That she was proud. That she had been wrong about the music, the friends, the years he spent far away. That she had loved him even when she didn’t know how to show it.

But he was sleeping, and she was glad. He had spent enough nights keeping watch.

Her thoughts drifted, gathering small things as they went: the smell of oranges in winter; the blue cup with a crack near the handle; her husband humming off-key while he washed dishes. She had once believed a life would be measured by its grand moments. Now she thought it might be measured by the ordinary ones that had stayed.

The rain softened. Somewhere outside, a car passed through a puddle.

Mara tried to lift her hand. Her son woke at once and caught it in both of his.

“I’m here,” he whispered.

She wanted to tell him that he didn’t have to be. That he could go on now, without guilt. That leaving was not the same as being left.

Her lips moved, but no words came.

So she gave his fingers the faintest squeeze.

He understood—or perhaps he simply hoped he did. Either way, his face eased.

Mara watched the lamp glow against the wall. Its circle of light was small, but it was enough to see the room: the sleeping flowers on the sill, the books stacked crookedly, her son’s hand around hers.

Her last thought was not of what she had lost, nor of what waited beyond the dark.

It was this: *How lucky I was to have been here.*

prompt: A case hinges on something witnessed only by a dead person . To illustrate how ludicrous this is , one side subpoenas the dead person . The dead person shows up and testifies .
content:
### The Subpoena

The case of Bell v. Bell concerned a bakery, a will, and one sentence spoken beneath a pear tree in 1986.

The bakery had been founded by Elias Bell, who left it to his two sons—unless, as his former apprentice Mara claimed, he had already promised it to her. The promise had never been written down. No letter, no note, no recording. There had been just two people beneath the pear tree that afternoon: Elias and his brother Arthur.

Arthur had been dead for eighteen years.

At the first hearing, Mara’s lawyer stood and said, “My client’s claim depends on the testimony of the only witness to the conversation.”

The judge peered over her glasses. “And that witness is?”

“Arthur Bell, Your Honor.”

A silence settled over the courtroom.

The sons’ lawyer, Mr. Voss, gave a little laugh. “Then I move we subpoena him. It will demonstrate, quite neatly, the absurdity of this claim.”

The judge considered this. “If you are certain.”

“I am.”

“Very well.”

The clerk prepared the subpoena. Since Arthur had no forwarding address, it was delivered to the cemetery, where the groundskeeper signed for it with some reluctance.

On the day of trial, Mr. Voss began his argument.

“Ladies and gentlemen of the court, we are being asked to decide a living person’s property rights on the basis of a conversation no living person heard—”

The courtroom doors opened.

An old man entered, brushing leaves from the shoulders of his dark suit. He was pale, but not especially transparent. He carried a folded copy of the subpoena.

“Arthur Bell?” asked the bailiff.

“That’s what it says.”

The judge removed her glasses. “You are aware you’ve been called to testify?”

“I’ve been aware of it since Tuesday,” Arthur said. “The groundskeeper read it aloud. He has a very good voice.”

Mr. Voss stood slowly. “Your Honor, I would like the record to reflect that the witness is deceased.”

“It may reflect whatever it likes,” said the judge. “Please swear him in.”

The clerk hesitated. “Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?”

Arthur raised one hand. “I do.”

“On what authority?” Mr. Voss demanded.

Arthur looked at him. “The same one you’re using.”

The judge hid a smile behind her papers.

Mara’s lawyer asked the first question. “Were you with your brother Elias beneath the pear tree on the afternoon of April 12, 1986?”

“Yes.”

“Did he tell you he intended to give the bakery to Mara?”

“He did.”

Mr. Voss rose for cross-examination. “Mr. Bell, you’ve been dead for eighteen years.”

“Twenty-one,” Arthur corrected. “You’re counting from the wrong spring.”

“Does being dead improve your memory?”

“No. But it does make certain conversations hard to forget. There aren’t so many new ones.”

Mr. Voss paced before the witness stand. “Isn’t it possible you’ve confused what Elias said with what you hoped he’d say?”

Arthur considered that. “I hoped he’d leave the bakery to me.”

A murmur went through the room.

“But he didn’t,” Arthur continued. “He said Mara had kept the ovens going through the strike, the flood, and the winter the boiler died. He said the bakery was hers if she wanted it. I asked him if he meant the building or the business. He said, ‘Both. Don’t make me say it twice.’”

“Conveniently remembered,” said Mr. Voss.

“Not convenient,” Arthur said. “I was annoyed about it for the next thirty-seven years.”

The judge leaned forward. “Did Elias ever change his mind?”

“Not that I heard.”

“And you’re certain of that?”

Arthur glanced at the sons, who sat with their hands folded on the table. “He told them too. They were there the next morning. They were young, but not so young they couldn’t understand the word ‘Mara.’”

Mr. Voss had no further questions.

The judge recessed for an hour. When she returned, she ruled that Arthur’s testimony was admissible. The sons appealed, but the appeal was dismissed on the grounds that they had been the ones who insisted he appear.

Afterward, in the courthouse hallway, Mara thanked Arthur.

He waved her off. “I didn’t come for thanks. I came because that fellow’s subpoena was rude.”

“Will you come by the bakery?” she asked.

“I can’t eat.”

“You can sit.”

Arthur looked toward the street, where the afternoon light lay warm across the pavement.

“I’ve had a long time to sit,” he said. “But I’d like to see the ovens.”

prompt: You 're a teenage boy who has to break the news to your parents that your girlfriend got you pregnant .
content:
**The Sentence**

I practiced in the bathroom mirror until the words stopped sounding like they belonged to somebody else.

“Mom, Dad, I’m pregnant.”

I tried again.

“My girlfriend got me pregnant.”

That sounded worse.

At seventeen, I’d already learned how to tell people I was a boy. Usually it went fine. Sometimes it didn’t. My parents had gotten it right from the beginning, even when they stumbled over my name or worried aloud about what the world would be like for me. I trusted them.

Trusting them didn’t make this easy.

My girlfriend, Lena, was waiting in the car outside. She’d offered to come in, but I’d asked her to give me a few minutes alone with them first. My hands shook as I came into the kitchen.

Mom was sorting the mail. Dad was trying to fix the toaster with a butter knife.

“Hey,” Mom said. “You okay?”

I sat down. “I need to tell you something, and I need you to let me finish before you say anything.”

Dad carefully set down the toaster.

Mom’s face changed. “All right.”

I stared at the wood grain of the table. “Lena and I took a test. Then we went to the clinic. I’m pregnant.”

The room went perfectly still.

Dad blinked. Mom’s hand covered her mouth. For one long second, I thought they hadn’t understood me.

Then Mom came around the table and crouched beside my chair. “Are you sure?”

I nodded. “The doctor confirmed it.”

“Oh, honey.”

Her voice broke, and that was somehow what made me cry. I’d been holding myself together for days, telling Lena we’d figure it out, telling myself I wasn’t scared. But Mom’s kindness unfastened something in me.

Dad pulled out a chair and sat. “How are you feeling?”

“Scared,” I said. “And confused. And I don’t know what we’re going to do.”

“That makes sense,” he said.

I wiped my face with my sleeve. “I’m still your son.”

Mom took my hand. “You have always been our son.”

Dad nodded, his eyes shiny. “This doesn’t change that.”

I looked between them, waiting for the questions, the anger, the lecture. They came—but not all at once, and not like weapons. They wanted to know what the doctor had said, whether Lena was safe, whether I had someone to talk to. They asked what I wanted. When I didn’t know, they said we could take time to find out.

At last, Dad asked, “Do you want Lena to come in?”

I nodded.

Mom went to the front door. Through the window I saw Lena climb out of the car, her shoulders hunched against the cold. She walked up the path slowly, like she was giving herself time to turn around.

When she came inside, Mom hugged her too.

We sat together at the kitchen table—the four of us, with the broken toaster still in pieces beside Dad’s elbow. Nobody had a perfect plan. Nobody pretended the next months would be simple.

But when Lena took my hand, my parents stayed beside us.

For the first time since I’d seen the test, I could breathe.

{prompt}
prompt: You are a child who experienced a nightmare about a werewolf . Now , in every sleep , you experience the same nightmare . You have the choice to claim victory or defeat to end your recurring dream .
content:
The first time I dreamed of the werewolf, I was six.

It stood at the end of a moonlit path, taller than the trees, with yellow eyes and a mouth full of silver teeth. I ran until my legs hurt. I ran until the trees blurred and the moon followed me like a lantern. Then the werewolf caught my shadow.

I woke up screaming.

After that, the dream came every night.

It didn’t matter if I slept with the hall light on or tucked my stuffed rabbit beneath my chin. The path was always there. The moon always watched. And the werewolf always waited at the end.

As I got older, I learned the dream’s rules. I could run, but never escape. I could shout, but no sound came out. And when the werewolf lunged, I always woke just before its claws reached me.

Then, on the night I turned ten, the dream changed.

The werewolf stood in its usual place, but this time I didn’t run. Maybe I was tired of running. Maybe I was tired of waking my parents.

It lowered its head. Its claws pressed into the dirt.

“You know how this ends,” it growled.

Behind it, the path split in two. One trail led into darkness. The other climbed toward the moon, bright as a strip of snow.

A voice spoke from somewhere above me. “Choose. Claim victory, or claim defeat. Either will end the dream.”

The werewolf smiled, showing every tooth.

“Defeat,” it said. “You’re frightened. You’ll always be frightened.”

I thought of all the mornings I’d woken up shaking. All the nights I’d begged for someone to leave the light on. The werewolf had been right about one thing: I was frightened.

But being frightened wasn’t the same as losing.

I took one step toward it.

The werewolf snarled. “You can’t beat me.”

“I don’t have to,” I said. My voice came out small, but it came out. “You’re only in my dream.”

Its smile vanished.

I looked up at the moon. It seemed close enough to touch. Then I looked back at the werewolf, and for the first time I saw something besides teeth and claws. Its ears were pinned back. Its paws trembled in the dirt.

It was scared, too.

“I claim victory,” I said.

The word rang through the trees. The werewolf shrank—not into a little boy, or a pet dog, or anything friendly. It simply grew smaller, until it was no taller than me. Then the path, the trees, and the moon folded away like a picture in a book.

I woke in my bed.

The room was dark. My rabbit was beside me. My heart beat fast, but I wasn’t screaming.

That night, I dreamed of a beach instead. The waves rolled in and out, and the moon made a silver road across the water.

I still get scared sometimes.

But I don’t dream of the werewolf anymore.

prompt: Professor Paradox manipulates time so that his defeat would cause a paradox
content:
### The Last Second

The clock tower had no hands.

Instead, a silver ring revolved around its face, ticking backward through the numbers. Every time it passed twelve, the city below shuddered: cars jumped a few feet down the street, rain climbed toward the clouds, and a flock of pigeons flew backward into the sky.

Ben stared up at it. “So, just to be clear, this is the part where we stop the weird clock?”

“Not quite,” said Professor Paradox. He stood on the tower’s balcony, immaculate as ever, one gloved hand resting on a brass device that pulsed with blue light. “This is the part where you try.”

Gwen narrowed her eyes. “You did this.”

“I did,” Paradox agreed. “Though ‘did’ is an imprecise word when one has been editing the past.”

Kevin cracked his knuckles. “Then we’ll edit you out of the present.”

He lunged.

The instant Kevin’s fist struck Paradox, the world went white.

Ben blinked—and found himself standing at the foot of the tower again. Kevin was beside him, fist raised. The sky was full of pigeons, all flying forward.

“Again?” Ben said.

Kevin lowered his hand. “I haven’t even hit him yet.”

“You did,” Gwen said. She looked unsettled. “I remember it.”

Above them, Paradox leaned over the balcony. “You see the difficulty.”

Ben tapped the Omnitrix. “Then let’s try something else.”

He transformed into Four Arms and hurled a chunk of loose masonry. It sailed toward the balcony.

White light.

The tower. The pigeons. Kevin’s raised fist.

This time Ben didn’t move. “Every time we attack him, we reset.”

“Correct,” Paradox called down. “Your victory is the trigger.”

Gwen studied the silver ring circling the clock face. “You’ve tied your defeat to a point in the past.”

“Nicely observed.”

“If Ben beats you,” she continued, “the machine sends the moment backward. But if that moment never happens, then the machine was never activated.”

“And yet it is activated,” said Paradox. “A delightful contradiction, isn’t it?”

Kevin scowled. “You built a trap where you can’t lose.”

“I built a trap where losing me breaks time.”

Ben glanced at the backward-running rain. “How many times have we done this?”

Paradox’s smile faded just a little. “More than you remember.”

A tremor rolled through the street. For a moment, the buildings became transparent, showing older buildings beneath them—then newer ones, then empty foundations. The silver ring on the clock spun faster.

Gwen’s face tightened. “The loop’s getting unstable.”

“Time is not fond of being asked the same question forever,” Paradox said.

“Then shut it off,” Ben shouted.

“I can’t.”

“Why not?”

Paradox looked down at the device in his hand. “Because I constructed the loop around the moment of my defeat. The mechanism recognizes only one ending: you overcome me, and it sends me back to the beginning. I cannot stop it without causing the very event that activates it.”

Kevin gave a humorless laugh. “You trapped yourself.”

“I prefer ‘made myself indispensable.’”

Ben watched him carefully. “You’re not trying to win. You’re trying to make sure nobody can ever beat you.”

Paradox said nothing.

The clock rang. The sound came from everywhere at once. A crack split the air above the tower, revealing a starless blackness behind the sky.

Gwen stepped closer to Ben. “We have to break the device without attacking him.”

“Can we do that?”

“Maybe. But he has to let us.”

Ben looked up. “Professor! You said defeat causes the paradox. So what if we don’t defeat you?”

“And what,” Paradox asked, “would you call it when you stop me?”

“Your choice.”

For the first time, Paradox looked genuinely uncertain.

The clock rang again. The crack in the sky widened. A piece of the tower vanished, then reappeared a moment later, made of unfamiliar stone.

“You can keep this going,” Ben said. “Maybe forever. But sooner or later, the loop breaks everything. Or you can choose to turn it off.”

“And if I do,” Paradox said, “you will have won.”

“No,” Ben replied. “You’ll have stopped.”

The silver ring shuddered. Across the city, every clock began to strike at once.

Paradox looked at the device in his hand. “I spent centuries ensuring no one could take this decision from me.”

“Then don’t let the machine make it for you,” Gwen said.

For a long moment, the professor stood very still. Then he pressed his thumb against the brass device—not to activate it, but to open it.

The blue light went out.

The clock tower’s backward ring slowed. The crack in the sky drew closed. Rain fell normally. The pigeons swooped over the rooftops, bewildered but unharmed.

Paradox stepped down from the balcony and landed lightly on the street.

Kevin raised his fists. “So, are we done?”

Ben watched Paradox. “I think so.”

“Then I shall take my leave,” the professor said, adjusting his cuffs. “And, for the record, I was not defeated.”

Ben grinned. “Sure.”

Paradox vanished in a shimmer of blue.

Gwen glanced at the now-motionless clock. “Do you think he really chose to stop?”

Ben shrugged. “Does it matter?”

Above them, the clock face remained blank. For the first time, it had no way to tell what would happen next.

prompt: As you tend your large garden , you notice a naked couple walk unnervingly close to a tree bearing golden fruit ...
content:
Every morning, I walked the garden’s long paths with a tin watering can in one hand and a pair of shears in the other. The garden was too large for one person, but it had belonged to my family for generations, and I had never learned to imagine it without me.

At the far end stood the golden tree.

It grew behind a low wall of white stone, though no one remembered building the wall. Its leaves were dark green, almost black, and its fruit shone like small suns. I had never tasted one. My grandmother said the fruit was beautiful because it was forbidden, and forbidden because it was beautiful. She said this as if it explained anything.

That morning, I saw the couple.

They crossed the grass without a sound, a man and a woman, both naked and pale in the early light. They walked hand in hand, looking neither embarrassed nor afraid. I called out. They did not turn.

“Stop,” I shouted, and the word came out smaller than I meant it to.

They kept walking.

The man was smiling. The woman was watching the tree.

I hurried after them, but the paths stretched beneath my feet. Beds of lavender and rosemary slipped past on either side; the stone fountain dwindled behind me. The couple reached the wall. The woman laid her palm against it, and the stones parted like curtains.

I stopped at the opening.

“Those are not for you,” I said.

The woman looked back. Her eyes were so clear they seemed to contain no reflection at all.

“Then why do you keep them?” she asked.

I had no answer. I had spent my life pruning, watering, sweeping fallen leaves from the paths. I had counted the fruit each autumn and locked the gate each night. I had mistaken care for ownership so gradually that I no longer knew the difference.

The man reached toward a low branch.

I stepped through the wall.

The air beneath the tree was warm and smelled of rain. I caught his wrist just as his fingers brushed the fruit. His skin was cold.

“Don’t,” I said.

For the first time, the woman seemed frightened. Not of me, but for me.

“You’ve been here so long,” she whispered. “You’ve forgotten there was a gate.”

Then the golden fruit dropped.

It struck the grass without a sound. The man and woman vanished. The wall closed behind them. And somewhere beyond the garden, a door creaked open.

I bent to pick up the fruit.

It was warm in my hand. The gold came away on my fingers like dust.

For a long while, I stood beneath the tree, listening to the garden breathe. Then I set down my shears, walked back along the path, and left the gate unlatched.

prompt: Fear and The Emotions of Social Interaction ( Come Together )
content:
## The Space Between Hello and Goodbye

Mara’s fear had a chair of its own.

It was a little too small, with a crooked leg, and it always sat beside her whenever she entered a room full of people. On the evening of the neighborhood supper, Fear had taken the chair before Mara even got through the door.

“You can still leave,” it whispered.

Mara looked through the open doorway. Inside, neighbors carried bowls and platters between folding tables. Someone laughed loudly. Someone else called her name.

She tightened her grip on the dish she’d brought.

“I know,” she whispered back.

Fear leaned closer. “You don’t have to explain yourself. You don’t have to say anything. We could go home, put on soft socks, and never think about this again.”

That sounded wonderful. It also sounded lonely.

Mara stepped inside.

At once, the other feelings appeared. Joy came bounding over, bright as a string of lights. Curiosity followed, peering at the crowded room as if it were a museum. Embarrassment ducked behind Mara’s shoulder, already blushing. Anger folded its arms.

“Everyone will notice you don’t know what to do,” Fear said.

“Maybe,” said Curiosity. “But maybe we’ll find out what’s in that pie.”

“I don’t want to make a fool of myself,” Mara said.

Embarrassment gave a sympathetic nod. “I’m afraid we may.”

Anger frowned at Fear. “You always make it sound like a disaster is the only possibility.”

“And you always think shouting will help,” Fear replied.

“Enough,” said Sadness, who had arrived quietly and stood beside Mara. “She’s allowed to feel all of this.”

For a moment, the feelings went still.

Mara took one step toward the tables. Then another.

A woman with silver hair looked up from arranging napkins. “You must be Mara. I’m June.”

Mara opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

Fear tightened its little fingers around her sleeve.

Then Joy nudged her. Curiosity waited. Embarrassment stood close, but it didn’t hide. Even Anger seemed to understand that this was not the moment to win an argument.

“Hi,” Mara managed. “I brought apple cake.”

June smiled. “I’m glad you came. We’ve been hoping to meet you.”

It wasn’t a grand moment. No music swelled. Nobody applauded. June simply took the cake, found a place for it on the table, and asked Mara where she had learned to bake.

Mara answered. Her voice trembled at first, then steadied. She learned that June had a garden, that the boy at the next table was called Eli, and that someone had put cinnamon in the soup. When Mara didn’t know what to say, she asked a question. When she said something awkward, Embarrassment blushed, but the world did not end.

Fear stayed beside her throughout the evening.

It warned her when the room grew too loud. It made her notice when she needed a breath. Once, when a stranger asked a question that felt too personal, Fear helped Mara step away and join June by the window.

At the end of the supper, Mara carried an empty cake plate home. The feelings walked with her beneath the streetlights.

“So,” said Anger, “we survived.”

“We did more than survive,” said Joy.

Embarrassment peeked out from behind Mara’s shoulder. “I may have called Eli by the wrong name.”

“You did,” said Curiosity. “His name is Evan.”

Embarrassment groaned. “I knew it.”

Mara laughed. Fear looked up at the sound, surprised.

“You were there the whole time,” Mara said to it.

“Of course,” Fear replied. “I’m always there.”

“I know.” Mara reached for its hand. “But you don’t have to sit in the driver’s seat.”

Fear considered this. Then it climbed into the crooked little chair again, where it fit much better.

The feelings continued down the street together—not quiet, not perfectly in step, but moving in the same direction.

And next time, Mara thought, she might bring something besides cake.

prompt: You arrive in the year 1000 , and all you have are the clothes on your back , a laptop with the entire Wikipedia library , and a solar charger .
content:
## The Last Page

I arrived in a barley field under a sky so blue it seemed newly made.

My phone was gone. My wallet, keys, and shoes were gone. I had the clothes I’d been wearing, a laptop, and a foldable solar charger tangled around one wrist.

The laptop was warm. Its screen showed the familiar Wikipedia globe, and beneath it, every article I’d ever downloaded. The battery read 83 percent.

I checked the date on the system clock. It said 2024, which was no help. I searched for *year 1000*.

Then I heard a bell.

A man on horseback had stopped at the field’s edge. He wore a wool cloak and carried a spear. He called something I almost recognized. I answered in English, which made him look more alarmed.

By nightfall, I had learned that I was in England, near a place called Winchester, and that the year was, according to the monks, 1000. I had also learned that my accent made me sound like a foreigner, my clothes made me look like a lunatic, and the black glass rectangle in my hands made me look like either a sorcerer or a very bad liar.

The monks took me in because one of them had a cough and I told them he needed water, rest, and a clean place to sleep. I knew enough about medicine to be useful and not enough to be wise. I showed them how to boil water. I explained that washing hands mattered. They listened politely, then watched me as if I had asked them to worship a kettle.

My laptop became a book of wonders. I showed them maps, stars, diagrams of the human body. I tried to explain the size of the world, then the age of the world, then germs. The last one went badly. I had no microscope, no proof, only invisible creatures in an illuminated box.

“Can you show us these creatures?” the abbot asked.

“No,” I said.

He nodded, as though I had confirmed something.

I stopped trying to impress them. Instead, I searched the articles for things I could make useful: crop rotation, simple sanitation, the idea that a fever could spread from person to person. I couldn’t hand them a future. I could only offer small improvements, dressed in words they might accept.

The solar charger bought me time. On clear days, I set it on the roof and guarded it from curious hands. The laptop’s battery fell anyway. I rationed it: a few minutes each evening, one article at a time. I read about the place I stood, about the king, the monasteries, the languages changing beneath my feet. I read what the future said would happen.

I stopped reading the future after the first winter.

It was one thing to know that a king would die, that a battle would be lost, that a country would be conquered. It was another to know the names of people who were still alive, eating supper in the next room.

The abbot asked me to copy down what I knew. So I did—not the whole of Wikipedia, which was impossible, but a few pages of practical advice. I wrote about clean water, food storage, childbirth, stars, and how to keep a record of the harvest. My hand cramped. The parchment was precious. I left out the internet.

Years passed.

The laptop became a dark, smooth stone. I kept it wrapped in cloth, though I no longer knew why. The monks preserved my notes. Some ideas took root; others were copied and misunderstood, as ideas often are. A young novice learned to ask what evidence supported a claim. I told him that was a good question, though I could not explain where I’d learned it.

One morning, when I was old enough to be called an old man, he brought me a page from the library. It described the world as a sphere. In the margin, someone had written: *The stranger said this was so.*

I read the words twice.

Outside, bells rang over Winchester. The sun fell across the courtyard, bright on the stones. For a moment, I thought of the charger spread on the roof, drinking light for a machine that had once held every answer I could find.

Then I thought of the boy waiting for me to explain the page.

I closed the book.

“Let’s begin with what we can prove,” I said.

prompt: - A successful movie actor decides to go through and watch his older films . But , while watching , discovers odd things . Scenes he does n't remember , lines that were n't in the script , and interviews he never did . It 's in all his movies , and gets steadily more sinister .
content:
### The Uncredited Man

At fifty-two, Daniel Vale had made thirty-one films, won two awards he kept in a drawer, and learned to answer questions about his career without sounding bored.

When the Meridian Film Festival announced a retrospective, Daniel decided he ought to watch the films again. Not the famous ones, necessarily. All of them. In order. He told his publicist it was a way to prepare.

In truth, he wanted to know whether the boy in his first movie had ever been any good.

He began with *The Orchard*, shot when he was twenty-one. The film was grainy, all summer light and earnest dialogue. Daniel watched himself stumble through a scene as a waiter in a country hotel. He had no lines. He remembered the day: rain all morning, a broken coffee machine, the director shouting at someone named Paul.

Then, as Daniel crossed behind the leading couple, a woman at the end of the bar turned toward him.

“Not yet,” she said.

Daniel paused the film.

He rewound. The woman was there, her face blurred by the old print. He played it again.

“Not yet.”

He checked the script online. The role wasn’t listed. He checked the credits. No woman at the bar.

The next morning, he called the studio archivist. She said the restored version had been assembled from the original negative. No alterations. No alternate cut.

“Could be a line from the background,” she said. “You know how those things happen.”

Daniel did know. He let it go.

The second film had a stranger thing. In a kitchen scene, Daniel’s character asked his brother for the time. The brother replied, “You can stop pretending now.”

Daniel sat up.

The line wasn’t in the script. He found the shooting pages in a box in his office. The scene ended with the question about the time. No answer.

He searched his memory for the set. For the actor playing his brother. He remembered the man’s name, his laugh, the smell of the fake kitchen’s hot lights. He didn’t remember that line.

He watched the scene again.

“You can stop pretending now.”

By the time he reached his fifth film, the oddities had become a game. A woman in a red scarf standing in the back of a courtroom. A taxi driver saying, “You were late,” though Daniel’s character had arrived early. A shot in which Daniel looked past his scene partner and directly into the lens.

He’d never noticed how often he did that.

On the old behind-the-scenes featurette for *The Glass Harbor*, Daniel found an interview he didn’t remember giving. He was twenty-nine, wearing a blue sweater, sitting beneath a palm tree. The interviewer asked what he hoped to do next.

The young Daniel smiled. “I think I’d like to stop being watched.”

The interviewer laughed. “You mean take a break?”

“No,” Daniel said. “I mean stop being watched.”

The featurette cut to a shot of the director explaining the film’s ending.

Daniel checked the date. He was sure he’d never done the interview. His publicist had a folder of press itineraries from the time. No interview with that outlet. He called the director, now living in Portugal.

“Does that sound like me?” Daniel asked.

The director was quiet a moment.

“It sounds like something you’d say,” he finally replied.

Daniel didn’t sleep well that night.

He stopped watching for three days. Then he started again, telling himself that the mind was a machine for making patterns. He watched *The Last Passenger*, his first major success, and found a scene he did remember: his character alone in a train compartment, speaking to his reflection in the window.

Except the reflection didn’t match him.

For half a second, it showed a man with gray at his temples, older than Daniel had been when he filmed it. The man wore Daniel’s face. He was looking not at his own reflection, but straight out of the screen.

Daniel froze the image. The pixels broke apart. He scrubbed back and played it again.

The reflection matched.

He watched the rest of the film with every light in the room on.

After that, the man appeared in every movie.

Sometimes he was only a shape in the background: standing beneath a streetlamp, seated in a theater, watching from the far end of a corridor. Sometimes he was clearer. A man in a dark coat, eyes fixed on Daniel. In the oldest films, he was young. In the later ones, he aged.

In a film from ten years ago, the man stood at the edge of a crowded party, gray-haired and pale. Daniel, onscreen, turned toward him. For a moment, the scene seemed to hold its breath.

Then Daniel’s character said, “I know you.”

The man in the coat disappeared behind a passing waiter.

Daniel called the festival and said he was sick. Then he called the archivist and asked for the uncompressed files from his most recent movie, *The Quiet House*. She sent them that afternoon.

He watched alone, in his screening room.

The film was set in a winter hotel. Daniel played a widowed pianist who returned there to settle his wife’s estate. He remembered the shoot clearly: long days, snow machines, a cracked piano bench. He remembered every scene.

At the end of the film, his character walked down an empty hotel corridor and entered a small screening room. This wasn’t in the theatrical version Daniel owned. He leaned forward as his younger self stepped into the room and sat among the dark rows.

Onscreen, the projector flickered to life.

The film playing on the screen was *The Orchard*.

Daniel felt the room grow cold.

The young man onscreen watched the old film. He watched himself cross behind the couple at the hotel bar. He watched the woman turn.

“Not yet,” she said.

Then the young Daniel looked over his shoulder, toward the camera.

“You can stop pretending now,” he said.

The picture cut to black.

Daniel stood and reached for the remote. Before he could press anything, the screen brightened again.

The man in the dark coat sat in the screening room. Not the character. Not the young Daniel. The older man from the reflections: gray at the temples, lines around the mouth. He sat in the row behind Daniel’s character, looking directly at the camera.

At Daniel.

The man spoke.

“You’ve seen enough.”

Daniel dropped the remote. It struck the floor and the film paused. The image held: the man’s face, one hand lifted as if to shield his eyes from light.

Daniel backed out of the room.

He went home, locked the doors, and slept with the television unplugged.

The next morning, he called the studio and told them to pull every copy of *The Quiet House*. He called his publicist and told her to cancel the retrospective. Then he opened his laptop and searched for the uncompressed file he’d watched.

It was gone.

For the next week, Daniel avoided screens. No television. No phone unless he had to. He put a blanket over the mirror in his bedroom.

On the eighth night, he woke to a sound from the basement.

A projector clicking.

He had never owned a projector. He stood at the top of the stairs and listened. The sound continued: a quick, steady flutter. Then light spilled up from below.

Daniel went down.

The screening room was empty. The projector sat on its table, running. On the screen was the interview from *The Glass Harbor*. Young Daniel beneath the palm tree. The interviewer was outside the frame.

“Do you think an actor can ever disappear into a role?” the unseen interviewer asked.

Young Daniel stared at the camera.

“Not if someone remembers him,” he said.

The image jumped. For a fraction of a second, the screen showed the empty room from behind the projector.

Daniel was standing in it.

He turned.

The room behind him was dark. The projector clicked on.

Onscreen, his image took a seat in the front row. Then it looked up, directly at him.

A voice came from the speakers.

“Not yet.”

prompt: You find a maintenance hatch to Earth .
content:
### The Earth Hatch

The hatch was behind a bank of water filters, where no hatch had any business being.

I found it because the filters were making a noise like a spoon dragged around the inside of a glass. I shut down the pump, slid between the pipes, and saw a small brass wheel set into the wall. Above it, someone had scratched a single word:

**EARTH**

I laughed. On the Moon, everything old was somebody’s joke. There were doors painted on walls, warning signs for machines that had been scrapped before I was born, even a plaque in the cafeteria claiming the coffee was made with “authentic terrestrial beans.”

Still, I turned the wheel.

The hatch opened inward.

Warm air touched my face. It smelled of wet leaves.

Beyond it was a narrow stairway, descending into darkness. I fetched a lamp and a tether, then called Control.

“Maintenance hatch behind the east filters,” I said.

“Which hatch?”

“The one labeled Earth.”

A pause. “There’s no hatch behind the east filters.”

I stepped through before they could tell me not to.

The stairs ended at a concrete landing. A door stood open at the bottom. On the other side, rain fell beneath a gray sky.

I knew Earth from pictures. Blue and white, bright as a jewel. But this was a city street, cracked down the middle and crowded with grass. A bus lay on its side beneath a tree. Water ran along the curb, carrying yellow leaves toward a storm drain.

I had been born under a dome, where rain came from sprinklers and every tree had a number.

I took one step outside.

The air was heavy and sweet. Somewhere, a bird made a sound so complicated I forgot to breathe.

My mother had told me Earth was dead. Everyone had. Dead, or dying, or too dangerous to touch—depending on who was trying to explain why we lived beneath glass.

I walked to the bus. Its windows were broken. A child’s red mitten rested on one seat, faded almost pink. I picked it up and held it in my palm.

Behind me, the hatch gave a warning beep.

My tether had gone taut.

The radio crackled. “Come back immediately. We’re reading pressure loss.”

I looked at the street, the trees, the rain shining on the pavement. For a moment I wanted to keep walking until I found someone who could explain the mitten. Until I found a house with lights in it. Until Earth became more than a word on a wall.

Then I turned around.

At the hatch, I paused. On the lunar side, Control was shouting my name. On this side, rain tapped softly against the concrete.

I set the mitten on the landing, where it would stay dry, and climbed through.

The hatch shut behind me with a heavy, ordinary click.

Control sealed the corridor and sent a crew to inspect the wall. They found no hatch. No stairs. No trace of rain.

But for the rest of my shift, the filters ran quietly.

And in my pocket, tucked beside my tools, was a single yellow leaf.

prompt: You wait tables in a Southern bar with a cartoonishly sassy , gay , black cook and are best friends with his sister . A vampire walks in to have a drink of the new fake blood your bar sells . You can also hear people 's thoughts and you 're half human , half fairy . Who killed your grandmother ?
content:
### The Red Creek Special

At the Junebug, we served three things people came for: fried catfish, cold beer, and the chance to complain about their exes where their exes might hear.

I served all three. Darius Bell handled the kitchen, where he ruled over the fryer with a wooden spoon and an opinion about everybody’s shoes. He was my best friend Nia’s older brother, and he’d been telling me what to do since I was twelve.

“Table four needs another napkin,” he called through the pass-through.

“They have six.”

“They’re using them to wipe their hands. That is what napkins are for, technically, but I’m trying to create an atmosphere.”

Darius was a handsome man with a booming laugh, a quick tongue, and the sort of patience that made people confess things to him while he was basting ribs. He also had no patience at all for me.

“Your atmosphere smells like hush puppies,” I said.

“Then we are succeeding.”

That night, the Junebug was debuting its newest special: a deep-red drink called Red Creek. It was synthetic blood, made for vampires who wanted a night out without hunting in the parking lot. The distributor promised it tasted “almost alive.” Darius said it tasted like tomato juice with a trust fund.

I was carrying a tray of Red Creek when the front door opened.

The man who came in wore a charcoal coat, though the night was warm. He had pale skin, dark hair, and the calm, careful expression of someone who had learned that people noticed him staring.

The thoughts around me rose and bumped together: *That’s a vampire.* *He’s handsome.* *Don’t say vampire; it’s rude.* *I wonder if he can hear us.*

I could hear them all.

I had been hearing people’s thoughts since childhood, when I was still small enough to hide under my grandmother’s kitchen table. Grandma said it was because I was half human and half fairy, though she usually added this while handing me a biscuit, as if the matter were no stranger than the weather.

The man sat at the counter.

“Red Creek?” I asked.

“That’s what I came for.”

His voice was low and polite. His thoughts were not.

*Please taste like the old recipe.*

I stopped.

“Something wrong?” he asked.

“Not yet.”

His eyes sharpened.

I brought him the glass. He took one sip, then closed his eyes. For a moment, all I could hear from him was a memory: rain on a tin roof, a woman laughing, the smell of honeysuckle.

My grandmother used to smell like honeysuckle.

“You knew her,” I said.

The vampire put down the glass.

Behind me, Darius called, “If this is a romantic reunion, please keep it away from the bar. We charge extra for drama.”

The man looked at me. “Your grandmother made this.”

“She’s been dead for twenty years.”

“I know.”

I heard the thought beneath his words: *I should have stopped him.*

Before I could ask who *him* was, the door opened again. Sheriff Bell came in, his hat brim dark with rain. He had been sheriff for as long as I could remember. He’d been the first person to tell me my grandmother’s death was an accident.

His thoughts reached me before he reached the counter.

*The vampire. The girl. Don’t let them talk.*

Then, clear as a bell:

*The iron knife is still under the porch.*

My tray tilted. Glasses rattled.

Nia, who was wiping down a table beside me, caught the edge before it fell. She looked at my face. “What?”

“Sheriff Bell killed my grandmother.”

The room seemed to shrink around the words.

Sheriff Bell’s hand moved toward his belt. Darius stepped out of the kitchen carrying a cast-iron skillet.

“I’d strongly recommend,” he said, “that you keep your hands where the nice people can see them.”

The sheriff gave a brittle laugh. “This is ridiculous.”

The vampire stood. “No,” he said. “It is overdue.”

His name, I learned later, was Silas. He had been passing through town the night my grandmother died. He’d seen the sheriff leaving her house with a bloodied sleeve. He’d been young then, frightened, and still believed that staying out of human trouble was the same as doing no harm.

Grandma had been murdered because she refused to tell Sheriff Bell where the old fairy crossing lay. He wanted to sell the land to a developer. She told him there were some doors people ought to leave shut.

The sheriff lunged for the door.

I heard what he meant to do a heartbeat before he did it: *Get to the truck. Get the knife. Finish this.*

Nia yanked the fire alarm.

The Junebug erupted in noise. Darius swung the skillet—not at the sheriff, but at the hat in his hand. It flew off and landed in a basket of cornbread. Sheriff Bell stumbled, and Silas caught him by the collar.

By the time the deputies arrived, Sheriff Bell was sitting at the bar, handcuffed, with cornbread crumbs on his shoulder.

“Should’ve ordered the catfish,” Darius said. “It’s harder to get crumbs in your hair.”

Outside, rain tapped against the windows. I stood beside Silas and looked down at the Red Creek in his glass.

“Did it taste like her recipe?” I asked.

“Almost,” he said.

“What was missing?”

He considered. “A little more sugar.”

I smiled despite myself. Grandma had always said people were too quick to put bitterness in things.

At the Junebug, Darius rang the dinner bell. Nia squeezed my hand. And for the first time in twenty years, when I thought of my grandmother, I didn’t hear the echo of a question.

I heard her laugh.

prompt: You wake up in a pile of hay , you are the infamous Wizard of the Beer .
content:
I woke up in a pile of hay with a chicken staring into my face.

“Are you the Wizard of the Beer?” she clucked.

I pushed a straw out of my mouth. My pointy blue hat was missing, my robes smelled like a brewery, and someone had tied a wooden spoon to my belt. “I am,” I said, though I wasn’t entirely sure. “Infamous, apparently.”

The chicken nodded gravely. “Then you’re just the wizard we need.”

She led me beyond the barn, where a line of animals waited beside a dry stone well. A donkey wore a tiny crown. Three rabbits held mugs. Even the old farm dog had come, though he looked more interested in the cheese platter than the magic.

“Our village festival is tonight,” said the donkey. “But the great barrel has gone dry.”

I raised my hands. They were sticky with something that might have been honey. “Have you tried asking the brewer?”

“We did,” said the chicken. “He’s the one who lost the barrel.”

I followed them to the village square. In the middle stood an enormous wooden barrel, empty as a politician’s promise. Beside it, a nervous brewer wrung his hands.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “I was trying to make a new kind of ale. I added one little spell, and the whole batch vanished.”

“Which spell?” I asked.

He swallowed. “The one for making things disappear.”

I stared at him. “That’s a very poor choice of spell for a brewer.”

“I know that now.”

I climbed onto the barrel and peered inside. Nothing but darkness—and, far below, a faint golden glow. I tapped the wood with my spoon. The barrel rumbled.

“Ah,” I said. “The beer hasn’t vanished. It’s hiding.”

“Why would beer hide?” asked a rabbit.

“Because,” I said, “you’ve all been calling it ‘the great barrel.’ It thinks it’s expected to be great.”

I put my ear to the barrel and spoke gently. “You don’t have to be great. You just have to be beer.”

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then came a burble.

The barrel shivered. Foam spilled over the rim, followed by a cheerful stream of amber ale. The villagers cheered. The brewer hugged the barrel. The chicken tried to hug me, but I was too tall, so she pecked my boot instead.

That evening, the festival filled the square with music and lantern light. Someone found my hat in the hay, and the donkey crowned me with the tiny one he’d been wearing.

“Tell us, Wizard,” said the chicken. “How did you learn such powerful magic?”

I took a sip from my mug.

“Experience,” I said.

Then I glanced at the brewer, who was carefully labeling a fresh barrel *NOT A DISAPPEARING BEER*, and added, “And a few unfortunate mistakes.”

The villagers laughed. The band struck up a tune. And for the first time in a long while, I felt less infamous than welcome.

“Hmm, kitten…”

Mara leaned over the cardboard box on her doorstep. Inside, a tiny gray kitten blinked up at her, one white paw resting on a folded note.

The note read: **I found her in the rain. She seems to have chosen you.**

“I don’t know anything about cats,” Mara told the kitten.

The kitten yawned.

“Strong argument.”

She brought it inside, dried its fur with a towel, and offered it a saucer of milk. The kitten sniffed the milk, then climbed straight into Mara’s lap and fell asleep.

Mara glanced toward the empty chair across the room—the one where her grandfather used to sit, telling stories about the strays he’d rescued over the years. She had missed those stories. She had missed him.

The kitten stirred, tucked its nose beneath Mara’s hand, and purred.

Mara smiled. “Hmm, kitten,” she whispered. “I suppose you’ll need a name.”

Outside, the rain eased to a drizzle. Inside, the little purr grew steadier, as if the house itself had remembered how to be warm.

content:
## Mission Compromised

“Mission compromised! Abort! Abort!”

The warning tore through Mara’s headset, loud enough to drown out the alarms.

She grabbed the edge of the console as the shuttle lurched. Beyond the cockpit glass, the planet rolled beneath them—a blue curve veiled in storm clouds. Somewhere below, in the ruins of the orbital station, her brother was waiting.

“Control, repeat!” she shouted.

Static answered. Then a voice, thin and frightened: “Mara, you have to come back. The station’s been breached.”

She looked at the countdown. Two minutes until the shuttle’s engines locked into descent. Two minutes until there was no turning around.

Her mission was simple: retrieve the station’s last survivor and escape before the failing reactor melted through the hull. Her brother had volunteered for the assignment. He’d joked that it was just another long shift.

“Abort,” Control said again. “That’s an order.”

Mara’s hand hovered over the return switch.

Then came a knock through the comms—not static, not an alarm. Three quick taps.

Their childhood signal.

“I’m here,” her brother said. “But I’m not alone.”

On the station camera, a figure appeared behind him. Not a person. Too tall, too still, its face hidden by the emergency lights.

Mara’s fingers curled around the switch.

“Control,” she said, “I’m aborting.”

The shuttle’s engines began to turn.

Her brother exhaled. “Good.”

She smiled grimly. “The mission, not the rescue.”

Mara cut the engines.

The shuttle dropped toward the station. And on the screen, her brother ran for the airlock.
